s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Article)
a. Article 16
b. Article 17
c. Article 18
d. Article 23
List-II (Subject)
i. Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
ii. Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
iii. Abolition of titles, except military and academic distinctions
iv. Abolition of untouchability
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Art. 16 – equality of opportunity in public employment (a-ii); Art. 17 – untouchability abolished (b-iv); Art. 18 – titles abolished except military and academic distinctions (c-iii); Art. 23 – prohibits human trafficking and forced labour, under the Right against Exploitation (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 14 is available to all persons, citizens as well as foreigners.
2. Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29 are available only to citizens.
3. Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish educational institutions.
4. Article 17 binds only the State and not private persons.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the ban on untouchability under Art. 17 applies to all and also binds private persons. Art. 14 covers all persons; Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29 are for citizens only; Art. 30 is the minorities' right to establish educational institutions.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Clause of Article 15)
a. 15(2)
b. 15(3)
c. 15(4)
d. 15(6)
List-II (Provision)
i. Access to shops, hotels, wells and roads – binds private persons too
ii. Special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs
iii. Special provisions for women and children
iv. Up to 10% reservation for EWS in education
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: 15(2) – access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, roads; it binds private persons as well as the State (a-i); 15(3) – women and children (b-iii); 15(4) – socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs (1st Amendment, 1951) (c-ii); 15(6) – EWS up to 10% in education (103rd Amendment, 2019) (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 15:
1. Clause (5) was inserted by the 93rd Amendment, 2005.
2. Reservation in admission under clause (5) extends to minority educational institutions referred to in Article 30.
3. Clause (4) was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: Art. 15(5) covers private aided or unaided institutions but excludes the minority institutions of Art. 30. 15(5) came by the 93rd Amendment (2005); 15(4) by the 1st Amendment (1951), after Champakam Dorairajan.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Clause of Article 16)
a. 16(3)
b. 16(4A)
c. 16(4B)
d. 16(5)
List-II (Provision)
i. Carried-forward backlog vacancies treated as a separate group
ii. Office in a religious institution may be kept for persons of that religion
iii. Reservation in promotion for SCs and STs
iv. Parliament may prescribe a residence requirement for certain jobs
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: 16(3) – only Parliament may prescribe residence requirements (a-iv); 16(4A) – SC/ST reservation in promotion (77th, 1995; 85th, 2001) (b-iii); 16(4B) – backlog vacancies a separate group, outside the 50% ceiling (81st, 2000) (c-i); 16(5) – office in a religious or denominational institution (d-ii).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. 'Descent' and 'residence' are prohibited grounds under Article 16(2) but not under Article 15(1).
2. Article 16(4B) on carried-forward vacancies was inserted by the 81st Amendment (2000).
3. Consequential seniority for SC/ST promotions under Article 16(4A) was added by the 77th Amendment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: the 77th Amendment (1995) first provided reservation in promotion; consequential seniority came with the 85th Amendment (2001). Art. 16(2) adds descent and residence to the Art. 15(1) grounds; 16(4B) is the 81st Amendment (2000).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 103rd Amendment, 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
2. It was passed as the 124th Constitution Amendment Bill.
3. The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the power of the States to identify socially and educationally backward classes.
4. Reservation for the economically weaker sections was introduced by the 102nd Amendment.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: EWS reservation (up to 10%) came by the 103rd Amendment; the 102nd gave the NCBC constitutional status. The 105th (2021) reversed the Maratha-case reading of the 102nd and restored the States' power to identify SEBCs.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Article)
a. Article 340
b. Article 338B
c. Article 342A
d. Article 335
List-II (Content)
i. SC/ST claims consistent with efficiency of administration
ii. National Commission for Backward Classes
iii. President appoints a commission on the conditions of SEBCs
iv. President specifies SEBCs for the Central List
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Art. 340 – commission on SEBCs (a-iii); Art. 338B – NCBC, given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (b-ii); Art. 342A – President specifies the Central List of SEBCs, States keep their own lists (c-iv); Art. 335 – SC/ST claims consistent with efficiency of administration (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 14:
1. 'Equality before law' is of British origin and is a negative concept.
2. 'Equal protection of the laws' is of American origin and is a positive concept.
3. Article 14 forbids reasonable classification but permits class legislation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is reversed: Art. 14 forbids class legislation, not reasonable classification. Equality before law (British, Dicey) is negative – no special privileges; equal protection (American, US 14th Amendment) is positive – like treated alike.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A valid classification under Article 14 needs an intelligible differentia and a rational nexus with the object of the law.
2. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, the Supreme Court said that equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies.
3. The view that any arbitrary State action violates Article 14 comes from Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, decided in 1980.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong only in the year: Maneka Gandhi was decided in 1978. The twin test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) and E.P. Royappa (1974) – equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies – are correct.

s:
Consider the following statements about recent Supreme Court rulings on equality:
1. In April 2026, the Court held that the State cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on dearness allowance without a valid classification.
2. In February 2026, in Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India, the Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the AICTE regulations.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1. Statement 2 is wrong: Mritunjay Tiwari (Feb 2026) concerned the UGC equity regulations, not AICTE. The April 2026 ruling (Kerala/KSRTC) held pensioners cannot be denied dearness allowance parity without valid classification.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Provision)
a. Article 361
b. Article 361A
c. Article 105
d. International law
List-II (Immunity)
i. President and Governors not answerable to courts
ii. Foreign sovereigns and ambassadors
iii. True, non-malicious report of legislative proceedings
iv. MPs for anything said or vote given in the House
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Art. 361 – President and Governors (a-i); Art. 361A (44th, 1978) – true, non-malicious reports of proceedings of Parliament/State legislatures (b-iii); Art. 105 – MPs (Art. 194 for MLAs) (c-iv); international law – foreign sovereigns, ambassadors, diplomats, UN agencies (d-ii).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 361:
1. A civil case against the President or a Governor can be instituted during the term only after two months' notice.
2. A criminal case may be started against the President during the term after two months' notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1. Statement 2 is wrong: no criminal proceedings may be instituted against the President or a Governor during the term at all; the two months' notice route applies only to civil cases.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Rule of Law:
1. A.V. Dicey set it out in 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution' (1885).
2. India borrowed the concept from the Government of India Act, 1935.
3. Dicey opposed the French droit administratif, under which officials were subject only to special administrative tribunals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: India borrowed the Rule of Law from Britain; the GoI Act 1935 gave the federal scheme, the Governor and emergency powers. Dicey's book is of 1885 and he opposed droit administratif.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Rule of Law in India rests primarily on Article 14.
2. It has been held a basic feature in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).
3. India adopted Dicey's third principle – rights flowing from judicial decisions – without modification.
4. Dicey's first element means regular law is supreme and no one is punished except for a distinct breach of law.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: India accepts Dicey's first two elements but reverses the third – in India the Constitution is the source of rights. The first element (absence of arbitrary power) does not mean the State has inherent unlimited police power.

s:
Assertion (A): Under the Rule of Law, the government itself is subordinate to law.
Reason (R): Under Rule by Law, the ruler stays above the law and uses law as a weapon of state control.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true, but R only describes the contrasting system (Rule by Law); it does not explain why under the Rule of Law the government is subordinate to law.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. 'Untouchability' is not defined in the Constitution or in the Act.
2. Article 17 operates against private individuals as well.
3. The Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act by an amendment of 1976.
4. After the renaming, the Act carries the year 1976 in its title.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the renamed Protection of Civil Rights Act keeps 1955 in its title. Untouchability is undefined, and Art. 17 also binds private individuals.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act:
1. It was enacted in 1989.
2. A non-SC/ST person who fabricates false evidence so that an SC/ST member is convicted of a capital offence gets imprisonment for seven years and fine.
3. If the innocent SC/ST member is executed as a result, the punishment is death.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: the punishment under Sec. 3(2)(i) is imprisonment for life and fine. The Act is of 1989, and if the innocent member is executed the punishment is death.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 18:
1. A citizen of India may accept a title from a foreign State with the consent of the President.
2. A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State needs the President's consent to accept a foreign title.
3. In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is wrong: under Art. 18(2) a citizen shall not accept a foreign title at all – there is no consent route. Art. 18(3) requires the President's consent for a non-citizen office-holder; Balaji Raghavan (Dec 1995) held the awards are not titles.

s:
Assertion (A): Article 18 is associated with social equality.
Reason (R): It ends artificial distinctions by barring the State from conferring titles other than military or academic distinctions.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: by abolishing titles (except military and academic distinctions) Art. 18 ends artificial distinctions, which is why it is counted among the provisions of social equality.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Item)
a. Social equality
b. Economic equality
c. Political equality
d. Ambedkar's 'inseparable trinity'
List-II (Provision / meaning)
i. Liberty, equality and fraternity
ii. Articles 325 and 326
iii. Articles 15, 17 and 18
iv. DPSP Article 39(b), (c) and (d)
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Social equality – Arts. 15, 17, 18 (a-iii); economic equality – DPSP Art. 39(b), (c), (d), not part of the FR to equality (b-iv); political equality – Arts. 325, 326 (c-ii); Ambedkar called liberty, equality and fraternity an inseparable trinity (d-i).

s:
Assertion (A): The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) inserted Article 15(4).
Reason (R): In Champakam Dorairajan, the Supreme Court struck down the Madras Communal Government Order under Article 29(2).
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: Art. 15(4) ('nothing in this Article or in clause (2) of Article 29 shall prevent the State…') was added by the 1st Amendment to overcome Champakam Dorairajan (1951).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
b. Samatha v. State of AP
c. Niyamgiri (Orissa Mining Corp.)
d. Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil
List-II (Holding)
i. No tribal land leases in Schedule V areas to non-tribals
ii. Gram Sabha's role under the Forest Rights Act, 2006
iii. Caste not the sole test; reservation generally below 50%
iv. Maratha quota struck down for crossing 50%
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Balaji (1962) – caste not the sole test, reservation generally below 50% (a-iii); Samatha (1997) – no leasing of Schedule V tribal land to non-tribals/private parties (b-i); Niyamgiri (2013) – Gram Sabha under the FRA, 2006, Dongria Kondh (c-ii); Jaishri Patil (2021) – Maratha quota struck for crossing 50% (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements about Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992):
1. It was decided by a nine-judge bench by a 6:3 majority.
2. It upheld 27% reservation for OBCs with the creamy layer excluded.
3. It permitted reservation in promotions.
4. It ordered a permanent body for backward classes, which led to the NCBC.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Indra Sawhney held there can be no reservation in promotions (the 77th Amendment then added Art. 16(4A)). The creamy layer and the 50% ceiling also originate in this case.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th, 81st and 85th Amendments subject to quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency of administration under Article 335.
2. Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) removed the need to prove backwardness of SCs and STs for reservation in promotion.
3. Jarnail Singh refused to apply the creamy layer principle to SC/ST promotions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: Jarnail Singh (2018) extended the creamy layer to SC/ST promotions. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th, 81st and 85th with the three conditions; Jarnail Singh dropped the proof of backwardness.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) upheld the 93rd Amendment and 27% OBC reservation in central institutions.
2. Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd Amendment by a 4:1 majority.
3. State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), by a 6:1 majority of seven judges, overruled E.V. Chinnaiah and allowed sub-classification of SCs and STs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: Janhit Abhiyan upheld the 103rd (10% EWS) by 3:2. Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) upheld the 93rd; Davinder Singh (1 Aug 2024, 7 judges, 6:1) overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).

s:
Consider the following statements about the 50% ceiling and the creamy layer:
1. The OBC creamy-layer limit fixed in 2017 is ₹8 lakh a year.
2. Carried-forward vacancies under the 81st Amendment are an exception to the 50% ceiling.
3. A State legislature is free to cross the 50% ceiling by law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: no State legislature has free power to cross the ceiling (the Maratha quota was struck down for this). The exceptions are carried-forward vacancies (81st), extraordinary situations and EWS 10%; the OBC creamy layer is ₹8 lakh (2017).

s:
Consider the following statements about the creamy layer in 2026:
1. In April 2026, Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy layer with the central income limits.
2. In August 2026, the Centre backed an income-based creamy layer for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1. Statement 2 is wrong: the Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs. Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy layer with the central limits in April 2026.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 19 originally guaranteed seven freedoms.
2. The Right to Freedom group consists of Articles 19 to 22.
3. The right to acquire, hold and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f) was deleted by the 42nd Amendment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: Art. 19(1)(f) (property) was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978, leaving six freedoms. Art. 19 originally had seven freedoms; the Right to Freedom group is Arts. 19–22.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Clause)
a. 19(1)(c)
b. 19(1)(d)
c. 19(1)(e)
d. 19(1)(g)
List-II (Freedom)
i. Reside and settle in any part of India
ii. Move freely throughout the territory of India
iii. Practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business
iv. Form associations, unions or co-operative societies
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: 19(1)(c) – associations, unions, co-operative societies (a-iv); 19(1)(d) – move freely throughout India (b-ii); 19(1)(e) – reside and settle (c-i); 19(1)(g) – profession, occupation, trade or business (d-iii).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 97th Amendment (2011) added the right to form co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c).
2. The same Amendment inserted Article 43B and Part IXB.
3. Freedom of conscience is one of the freedoms listed in Article 19(1).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: freedom of conscience is in Article 25, not Article 19(1). The 97th Amendment (2011) added co-operative societies to 19(1)(c), Art. 43B and Part IXB.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 20 gives protection in respect of conviction for offences.
2. Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.
3. Without the report of an Advisory Board, preventive detention under Article 22 may last up to six months.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: without an Advisory Board's report, preventive detention cannot exceed three months. Art. 20 – protection in conviction; Art. 21A – education, by the 86th Amendment (2002).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Sakal Papers (1961)
b. Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)
c. State of UP v. Raj Narain (1975)
d. Tata Press (1995)
List-II (Right read into Article 19(1)(a))
i. Freedom of the press including circulation
ii. Right to silence – not singing the National Anthem
iii. Right to information / right to know
iv. Commercial speech
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Sakal Papers (1961) – press and circulation (a-i); Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) – right to silence, with Art. 25 conscience (b-ii); Raj Narain (1975) – right to know (c-iii); Tata Press (1995) – commercial speech (d-iv).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Anuradha Bhasin (2020)
b. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)
c. PUCL (1997)
d. Naveen Jindal (2004)
List-II (Associated with)
i. Hoisting the National Flag
ii. Speech and trade over the internet
iii. No government monopoly over airwaves
iv. Safeguards against phone tapping
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) – internet speech and trade under 19(1)(a) and (g) (a-ii); Cricket Association of Bengal (1995) – telecast, no government monopoly on airwaves (b-iii); PUCL (1997) – phone-tapping safeguards (c-iv); Naveen Jindal (2004) – hoisting the National Flag (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Freedom of the press is implied in Article 19(1)(a).
2. Commercial speech was recognised as part of Article 19(1)(a) in Tata Press (1995).
3. The right to access the internet is linked to Article 21 and not to Article 19.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: internet access is linked to Article 19 (Anuradha Bhasin); privacy and shelter are the Art. 21 rights. Press freedom is implied in 19(1)(a); Tata Press (1995) recognised commercial speech.

s:
Assertion (A): Films may be pre-censored, unlike the press.
Reason (R): Films reach larger audiences.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: films may be subjected to pre-censorship, which the press is not, because they reach larger audiences.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Clause)
a. 19(3)
b. 19(4)
c. 19(5)
d. 19(6)
List-II (Grounds of restriction)
i. General public interest; protection of Scheduled Tribes
ii. Professional or technical qualifications; State monopoly
iii. Sovereignty and integrity; public order; morality
iv. Sovereignty and integrity; public order
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: 19(3), assembly – sovereignty and integrity, public order (not morality) (a-iv); 19(4), association – adds morality (b-iii); 19(5), movement/residence – general public interest, Scheduled Tribes (c-i); 19(6), profession – qualifications and State trade/monopoly (d-ii).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 19(2):
1. It provides eight grounds for restricting freedom of speech and expression.
2. In Kaushal Kishor (2023), the Supreme Court held these grounds to be exhaustive.
3. Sedition is one of the grounds listed in it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: sedition is not a 19(2) ground (nor are views opposing the Government or unbecoming criticism). There are eight grounds, and Kaushal Kishor (2023) held them exhaustive.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The First Amendment (1951) inserted in Article 19(6) the power to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to create State monopolies.
2. The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground of restriction.
3. 'Public order' was added to Article 19(2) by the Sixteenth Amendment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: public order (with friendly relations and incitement) came by the 1st Amendment, 1951. The 1st also rewrote 19(6); the 16th (1963) added sovereignty and integrity in 19(2), (3), (4).

s:
Consider the following statements about reasonable restrictions:
1. State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) laid down the test of reasonableness – nature of the right, purpose, extent and urgency of the evil, and proportionality.
2. Courts decide reasonableness, and a restriction must not eclipse the right itself.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: V.G. Row (1952) gave the test of reasonableness, and the courts – not the Government – decide whether a restriction is reasonable; it must not eclipse the right.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 19:
1. A company, as a legal person, cannot claim it, though its citizen shareholders may sue.
2. In Kaushal Kishor (2023), Articles 19 and 21 were held enforceable against non-State actors too.
3. A British citizen living in India can claim the freedom of trade and profession under Article 19(1)(g).
4. Articles 14, 19 and 21 form the 'golden triangle', linked in Maneka Gandhi (1978).
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Art. 19 is for citizens only, so a British citizen cannot claim 19(1)(g). Companies cannot claim it but citizen shareholders may; Kaushal Kishor extended Arts. 19 and 21 to non-State actors; Maneka Gandhi linked the golden triangle.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Kameshwar Prasad (1962)
b. All India Bank Employees' Assn (1962)
c. T.K. Rangarajan (2003)
d. CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar
List-II (Held)
i. Bandhs are illegal
ii. A demonstration is protected, a strike is not
iii. Strike is not a Fundamental Right
iv. Government employees have no right to strike
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Kameshwar Prasad (1962) – demonstration protected, not strike (a-ii); All India Bank Employees (1962) – strike only a legal right (b-iii); T.K. Rangarajan (2003) – no right of government employees to strike (c-iv); CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar – bandh illegal as it curbs others' freedoms (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The freedom of assembly under Article 19(1)(b) covers only peaceful and unarmed gatherings.
2. In May 2026, the Supreme Court said peaceful protest is everybody's right but must not disturb other citizens.
3. The right to strike is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: strike is not a Fundamental Right, only a legal right (All India Bank Employees, 1962). Armed gatherings are excluded from 19(1)(b); the May 2026 ruling says protest must not disturb others or occupy public space.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Centre has defended curbs under the FCRA by invoking Article 19(4).
2. In INSAF (2020), the Supreme Court held that any association may be barred from receiving foreign contributions.
3. Under Article 19(5), entry and settlement of outsiders may be limited to protect Scheduled Tribes.
4. There is no fundamental right to carry on a dangerous or immoral trade.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 3 and 4). Statement 2 is wrong: INSAF (2020) held that only associations in active politics may be barred from foreign funds. The Centre cites 19(4) for FCRA; 19(5) protects STs (Inner Line areas); no right to trades like trafficking.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Bennett Coleman (1972)
b. Aveek Sarkar (2014)
c. Shreya Singhal (2015)
d. Kedar Nath Singh (1962)
List-II (Ruling)
i. Sedition valid only for incitement to violence
ii. Newsprint policy fixing pages violated press freedom
iii. Community standards test for obscenity
iv. Section 66A of the IT Act struck down
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Bennett Coleman (1972) – newsprint/page policy (a-ii); Aveek Sarkar (2014) – community standards test (b-iii); Shreya Singhal (2015) – Sec. 66A struck as vague and overbroad (c-iv); Kedar Nath Singh (1962) – s.124A valid only for incitement to violence or public disorder (d-i).

s:
Assertion (A): In Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950), the ban on the journal Cross Roads was struck down.
Reason (R): 'Public order' was not then a ground of restriction under Article 19(2).
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: the ban failed because public order was not yet a 19(2) ground; the 1st Amendment (1951) then added it.

s:
Consider the following statements about Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020):
1. It held that internet shutdowns must be proportionate, temporary and published.
2. It recognised speech and trade over the internet under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) required shutdown orders to be proportionate, temporary and published, and protected internet speech and trade under 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).

s:
Consider the following statements about Articles 358 and 359:
1. After the 44th Amendment, Article 358 operates only when emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression.
2. Article 359 needs a Presidential order and suspends only the enforcement of the rights named.
3. Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended under Article 359.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: after the 44th Amendment, Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended. Art. 358 suspends Art. 19 automatically, only for war or external aggression (not armed rebellion); Art. 359 needs a Presidential order.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Subject)
a. Sedition (replaced)
b. Criminal defamation
c. Unlawful assembly
d. Prohibitory orders
List-II (New provision)
i. Section 163 BNSS
ii. Section 152 BNS
iii. Section 189 BNS
iv. Section 356 BNS
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Sedition (s.124A IPC) → s.152 BNS, endangering sovereignty, unity, integrity (a-ii); criminal defamation → s.356 BNS (b-iv); unlawful assembly (IPC s.141) → s.189 BNS (c-iii); prohibitory orders (CrPC s.144) → s.163 BNSS (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements about the new criminal laws:
1. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the IPC.
2. The BNSS, 2023 provides for a statutory Zero FIR.
3. The new laws came into force on 1 July 2023.
4. Hate speech is dealt with under Section 196 of the BNS.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: the new criminal laws came into force on 1 July 2024. BNS replaced the IPC, BNSS (which replaced the CrPC) gives the statutory Zero FIR, and hate speech is s.196 BNS.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002:
1. It was introduced in Parliament as the 93rd Amendment Bill.
2. It made free and compulsory education for children of 6 to 14 years a Fundamental Right.
3. It changed Article 45 to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years.
4. It deleted the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the Right to Property was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978). The 86th (93rd Bill, 2001) inserted Art. 21A (6–14 years), recast Art. 45 for children below six and added Art. 51A(k).

s:
Consider the following statements about the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009:
1. Under Section 3, every child of 6 to 14 years has a right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school.
2. The 25% quota of entry-level seats in unaided private schools applies to minority schools as well.
3. Funding under the Act is a concurrent responsibility of the Centre and the States.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: the 25% quota for weaker and disadvantaged groups applies to unaided private schools but not to minority schools. Section 3 gives the 6–14 right in a neighbourhood school; funding is shared – the Centre does not bear sole responsibility.

s:
Assertion (A): The right to education was recognised as a Fundamental Right by the Supreme Court even before the 86th Amendment.
Reason (R): In Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993), the Court read the right to education into Article 21.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: Mohini Jain (1992) held that the right to education flows from Art. 21, and Unnikrishnan (1993) made free education up to 14 years a right – before Art. 21A came in 2002.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Concept)
a. Ex post facto law
b. Autrefois convict
c. Testimonial compulsion
d. Prohibition against torture
List-II (Provision)
i. Article 20(2)
ii. Article 21
iii. Article 20(1)
iv. Article 20(3)
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: No ex post facto criminal law – 20(1) (a-iii); double jeopardy rests on autrefois convict – 20(2) (b-i); no compulsion to be a witness against oneself – 20(3) (c-iv); protection against torture is not in Art. 20 but read into Art. 21 (d-ii).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 20:
1. It is available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies.
2. The bar on heavier retrospective penalty in clause (1) applies only to criminal laws.
3. Clause (2) also bars departmental proceedings after a criminal conviction for the same act.
4. Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not testimonial compulsion under clause (3) (Kathi Kalu Oghad, 1961).
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Art. 20(2) applies only to proceedings before a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental or administrative proceedings. Art. 20 covers all persons; 20(1) is limited to criminal laws; Kathi Kalu Oghad excludes physical evidence from 20(3).

s:
Assertion (A): Parliament cannot make a criminal law with retrospective effect that convicts a person or enhances punishment.
Reason (R): Article 20(1) prohibits ex post facto criminal laws.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: an ex post facto law is a retrospective law, and Art. 20(1) bars conviction except for violating a law in force at the time and any penalty greater than that law allowed.

b. Parmanand Katara (1989)
c. Subhash Kumar (1991)
d. Vishaka (1997)
List-II (Right read into Article 21)
i. Protection from workplace sexual harassment
ii. Shelter
iii. Emergency medical aid

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Chameli Singh (1995) – shelter (a-ii); Parmanand Katara (1989) – emergency medical aid, followed by Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) (b-iii); Subhash Kumar (1991) – clean environment (c-iv); Vishaka (1997) – workplace sexual harassment (d-i).

Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Francis Coralie Mullin (1981)
b. M.H. Hoskot (1978)
c. Nilabati Behera (1993)
d. Sheela Barse (1983)
List-II (Right read into Article 21)
i. Compensation for violation of rights
ii. Free legal aid
iii. Live with human dignity
iv. Protection of women in police custody
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) – dignity (a-iii); M.H. Hoskot (1978) – free legal aid (b-ii); Nilabati Behera (1993) – compensation (c-i); Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983) – women in police custody (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 21:
1. Its protection is available to citizens as well as non-citizens.
2. The right to travel abroad was linked to personal liberty in Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967).
3. The right to marry a person of one's choice was upheld in Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006).
4. In Supriyo Chakraborty (2023), the Supreme Court held that there is an unqualified fundamental right to marry.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: Supriyo Chakraborty (2023) held there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such, though Art. 21 protects the choice of partner (Lata Singh, Hadiya).

s:
Consider the following statements about the right to privacy:
1. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) recognised it unanimously by a nine-judge bench.
2. Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy as a Fundamental Right.
3. A limit on privacy must satisfy legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality.
4. Govind v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1975) is a case on the right to property.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: Govind v. State of MP (1975) is a privacy case, not a property case. Puttaswamy (24 Aug 2017, 9:0) placed privacy in Art. 21 and Part III and overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh; the test is legality, legitimate aim, proportionality.

s:
Consider the following statements about the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2):
1. An arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest and may consult a lawyer of choice.
2. The safeguards also cover a civil arrest and the deportation of an alien.
3. Bail as of right is not guaranteed by Article 22.
4. In Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025), the Supreme Court said the grounds must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 3 and 4). Statement 2 is wrong: civil arrest, arrest on a court order and deportation of an alien fall outside these safeguards. Grounds and a lawyer of choice are guaranteed; bail as of right is not; Vihaan Kumar (2025) stressed meaningful communication of grounds.

s:
Consider the following statements about preventive detention:
1. It is detention without trial, on suspicion of future harmful acts.
2. It is justified for public order, but not for routine law and order.
3. The 44th Amendment cut the period of detention without an Advisory Board report to two months, and that limit is in force today.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: the 44th Amendment (1978) did seek to cut it to two months, but the clause was never notified, so three months still applies. Preventive detention is without trial and is justified for public order, not routine law and order.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 22:
1. The Advisory Board consists of High Court judges or persons qualified to be such judges.
2. Clause (5) requires the grounds of detention to be communicated and the earliest opportunity of representation to be given.
3. Under clause (7), the President prescribes the maximum period of preventive detention.
4. Parliament alone can make preventive detention laws on defence, foreign affairs and the security of India.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: under Art. 22(7) it is Parliament that fixes the maximum period and the Advisory Board procedure. Public order, security of a State and essential supplies are shared by Parliament and the States.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Law)
a. Preventive Detention Act, 1950
b. MISA, 1971
c. COFEPOSA, 1974
d. National Security Act, 1980
List-II (Note)
i. Detention up to 12 months without charges
ii. First preventive detention law; lapsed 1969
iii. Used in the Emergency; repealed 1978
iv. Smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Preventive Detention Act 1950 – the first, lapsed 1969 (a-ii); MISA 1971 – used in the Emergency, repealed 1978 (b-iii); COFEPOSA 1974 – smugglers and currency manipulators (c-iv); NSA 1980 – up to 12 months without charges (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The National Security Act was enacted in 1980 and allows detention up to 12 months without charges.
2. In January 2026, the Supreme Court held that in UAPA cases delay alone is a trump card for bail.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1. Statement 2 is wrong: the Court said delay alone is not a 'trump card' for bail under the UAPA (1967). The NSA (1980) permits detention up to 12 months without charges.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 21:
1. The expression 'procedure established by law' is taken from the Japanese Constitution.
2. Article 21 uses the expression 'due process of law'.
3. Capital punishment does not violate Article 21 (Bachan Singh, 1980).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: Art. 21 does not use the words 'due process of law' (an American concept); it says 'procedure established by law', from Japan. Bachan Singh (1980) upheld the death penalty in the 'rarest of rare' cases.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A.K. Gopalan (1950) treated Articles 19, 21 and 22 as separate provisions.
2. Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable.
3. A.K. Gopalan held that Article 21 protects against arbitrary legislative action as well.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: Gopalan held that Art. 21 protects only against the executive and that any procedure enacted by the legislature suffices; it was Maneka Gandhi that extended protection against arbitrary legislation, in effect reading in due process.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Maruti Shripati Dubal (1987)
b. Chenna Jagadeeswar (1988)
c. P. Rathinam (1994)
d. Gian Kaur (1996)
List-II (Ruling)
i. SC: Sec. 309 IPC unconstitutional
ii. SC: right to life does not include right to die
iii. Bombay HC: right to die part of Article 21
iv. AP HC: no right to die; Sec. 309 upheld
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Maruti Shripati Dubal – Bombay High Court, 1987 (a-iii); Chenna Jagadeeswar – Andhra Pradesh High Court, 1988 (b-iv); P. Rathinam (1994) struck Sec. 309 (c-i); Gian Kaur (1996) overruled Rathinam and upheld Sec. 309 (d-ii).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In Aruna Shanbaug (2011), passive euthanasia under High Court supervision was allowed.
2. Aruna Shanbaug (2011) upheld the living will (advance directive).
3. In Common Cause (2018), dying with dignity was held a Fundamental Right under Article 21.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: the living will was upheld in Common Cause (2018), not in Aruna Shanbaug. Aruna Shanbaug's plea was rejected but passive euthanasia under High Court supervision was allowed.

s:
Consider the following statements about attempted suicide:
1. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 in effect decriminalised it.
2. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force from 1 July 2024, has no general offence of attempted suicide.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 effectively decriminalised attempted suicide, and the BNS (in force 1 July 2024) contains no general offence for it.

s:
Assertion (A): Even during a National Emergency, the right to life and personal liberty cannot be suspended.
Reason (R): The 44th Amendment (1978) provided that the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: since the 44th Amendment, Arts. 20 and 21 are the only Fundamental Rights whose enforcement cannot be suspended under Art. 359; Arts. 14, 19 and 22 can be.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 25:
1. The freedoms in Article 25(1) are subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
2. Humanism is one of the grounds on which the freedom of religion may be restricted.
3. Prisoners do not lose their Fundamental Rights merely because of lawful detention (Sunil Batra).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: the grounds are only public order, morality and health (plus the other provisions of Part III) – humanism is not one. Sunil Batra held prisoners keep their Fundamental Rights.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Term in Article 25(1))
a. Conscience
b. Profess
c. Practise
d. Propagate
List-II (Meaning)
i. Declare one's beliefs openly
ii. Inner freedom, including to follow no religion
iii. Worship, rituals and ceremonies
iv. Spread one's beliefs – not a right to convert another
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Conscience – inner freedom to mould one's relation with God, including following no religion (a-ii); profess – declare openly (b-i); practise – worship, rituals, ceremonies (c-iii); propagate – spread beliefs, but not convert another, which would impinge on the other's freedom of conscience (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 25:
1. Under 25(2)(a), the State may regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religion.
2. Under 25(2)(b), the State may throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
3. For this purpose, 'Hindus' includes Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists and Parsis.
4. Wearing and carrying kirpans is deemed part of the profession of the Sikh religion.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Explanation II includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists in 'Hindus', but not Parsis. 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity, not spiritual belief; 25(2)(b) allows reform and temple entry; Explanation I covers kirpans.

s:
Consider the following statements about Article 23:
1. It is available to citizens and non-citizens, and protects against the State as well as private persons.
2. 'Begar' means involuntary forced labour without payment.
3. Under Article 23(2), the State must pay remuneration in every case of compulsory service.
4. While imposing compulsory service, the State may not discriminate on grounds of religion, race, caste or class.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes (military or social service) without paying in every case; it only may not discriminate on religion, race, caste or class.

s:
Assertion (A): Article 24 does not bar harmless or innocent work by children.
Reason (R): Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below 14 years only in factories, mines and other hazardous employment.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: the absolute prohibition of Art. 24 is limited to factories, mines and other hazardous employment, so harmless work is outside it.

s:
Consider the following statements about child labour:
1. Directive Principles in Articles 39(e) and 39(f) protect children against exploitation.
2. The Supreme Court dealt with child labour in hazardous work in M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996).
3. The international instrument prohibiting it is the UN Charter.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: the international instrument is the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989, Art. 32), not the UN Charter. Arts. 39(e), 39(f) and M.C. Mehta (10 Dec 1996) are correct.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Law)
a. Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act
b. Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act
c. Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act
d. POCSO Act
List-II (Year)
i. 1986
ii. 2005
iii. 1956
iv. 2012
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act – 1956 (a-iii); Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act – 1986 (b-i); Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act (NCPCR, SCPCRs) – 2005 (c-ii); POCSO – 2012 (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 2016 amendment renamed the 1986 Act the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act.
2. Under it, adolescents aged 14–18 are barred from hazardous work.
3. Trafficking falls under Section 143 of the BNS, and the victim's consent is immaterial.
4. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act was passed in 1979.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act is of 1976. The 2016 amendment renamed the Act and barred adolescents from hazardous work; trafficking is s.143 BNS, with consent immaterial.

s:
Consider the following statements about secularism in India:
1. It means equal respect for all religions and no discrimination on religious grounds.
2. Article 325 bars exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of religion.
3. The word 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 44th Amendment.
4. The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to include 'God' in the Preamble.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: 'Secular' was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). India has no official religion and gives equal respect to all; Art. 325 and the 1949 rejection of 'God' are correct.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian model of secularism:
1. It is based on principled distance and equal respect, unlike the Western model of strict separation.
2. Sarva Dharma Sambhava combines State neutrality with positive intervention for reform.
3. Its roots include the Karachi Resolution of 1931.
4. It bars any State aid to religious or minority institutions.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: unlike the Western (negative) model, Indian secularism allows aid (Haj, minority institutions). It rests on principled distance and Sarva Dharma Sambhava; roots go to the Karachi Resolution (1931) and Nehru Report (1928).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. S.R. Bommai (1994)
b. Abhiram Singh (2017)
c. Shakti Vahini (2018)
d. Amit Sahni (2020)
List-II (Holding)
i. Appeals to religion or caste a corrupt practice under Sec. 123(3) RPA
ii. Khap interference and honour killings illegal
iii. Public ways cannot be occupied indefinitely by protesters
iv. Secularism a basic feature; Art. 356 against anti-secular governments
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: S.R. Bommai (1994) – secularism basic feature, dismissal under Art. 356 (a-iv); Abhiram Singh (2017) – widened Sec. 123(3) RPA (b-i); Shakti Vahini (2018) – honour killings (c-ii); Amit Sahni (2020, Shaheen Bagh) – public ways (d-iii).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Provision)
a. Article 26
b. Article 27
c. Article 28(1)
d. Article 28(3)
List-II (Content)
i. No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
ii. Freedom to manage religious affairs
iii. No compulsion to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion
iv. Attendance at religious instruction in aided institutions voluntary
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Art. 26 – manage religious affairs (a-ii); Art. 27 – no taxes whose proceeds promote a religion (b-iii); Art. 28(1) – no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions (c-i); Art. 28(3) – voluntary attendance in recognised or aided institutions (d-iv).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 26 is guaranteed to religious denominations or their sections.
2. Like Article 25, the rights under Article 26 are subject to the other provisions of Part III.
3. Article 27 is available to all persons and bars taxes, but not fees.
4. Under Article 28(3), a minor may attend religious instruction only with the guardian's consent.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 3 and 4). Statement 2 is wrong: Art. 26 is subject only to public order, morality and health – not to the other provisions of Part III, unlike Art. 25. Art. 27 binds for all persons and covers taxes, not fees; 28(3) needs a guardian's consent for a minor.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 27 and 28(1) are regarded as State-neutrality provisions.
2. Article 26 protects the individual's freedom of religion, while Article 25 protects the collective freedom.
3. In May 2026, the Supreme Court left it to the Ministry of Education whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is reversed: Art. 26 protects collective freedom (of denominations) and Art. 25 the individual's. Arts. 27 and 28(1) are State-neutrality provisions; the 12 May 2026 order is correct.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Shirur Mutt (1954)
b. Ramji Lal Modi (1957)
c. Rev. Stanislaus (1977)
d. Javed (2003)
List-II (Holding)
i. Polygamy not an essential religious practice
ii. Sec. 295A IPC upheld on public-order grounds
iii. Right to propagate is not a right to convert
iv. Origin of the Essential Religious Practice test
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Shirur Mutt (1954) – ERP test, defined 'religious denomination' (a-iv); Ramji Lal Modi (1957) – s.295A upheld (b-ii); Rev. Stanislaus (1977) – propagate ≠ convert, upheld Orissa and MP Acts (c-iii); Javed (2003) – polygamy not an ERP (d-i).

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Section 295A of the IPC now corresponds to Section 299 of the BNS.
2. The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, an early anti-conversion law, was enacted in 1967.
3. In St. Stephen's (1992), minority institutions were held to keep their autonomy, subject to regulation.
4. Instant triple talaq was declared invalid in Shayara Bano (2019).
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: Shayara Bano was decided in 2017. s.295A → s.299 BNS; Orissa Act 1967 (upheld in Stanislaus, which did not strike these laws down); St. Stephen's kept minority autonomy subject to regulation.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Sabarimala judgment (Indian Young Lawyers Association, 2018):
1. It was delivered on 28 September 2018 by a five-judge Bench by 4:1.
2. It held Ayyappa devotees to be a separate religious denomination.
3. It held that the exclusion of women of a certain age group is not an essential religious practice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 2 is wrong: the Court held Ayyappa devotees are not a separate religious denomination. The 5-judge Bench (4:1) struck down the age bar and held the exclusion not an ERP.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In 2022, the Karnataka High Court held that wearing the hijab is not an essential religious practice.
2. The nine-judge Bench hearing the 2026 review on the ERP doctrine is headed by CJI Surya Kant.
3. Punjab's Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act (2026) provides up to ten years' imprisonment for sacrilege.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: the Punjab Act (Apr 2026) provides up to life imprisonment for sacrilege. The Karnataka HC (2022) hijab ruling and the nine-judge Bench under CJI Surya Kant are correct.

s:
Consider the following statements about Census 2011:
1. Hindus formed 79.8% of India's population.
2. Muslims, at 14.2%, were the largest religious minority.
3. Christians formed 1.7% of the population.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: Christians were 2.3%; 1.7% is the share of Sikhs (Buddhists 0.7%, Jains 0.4%). Hindus 79.8% and Muslims 14.2% are correct.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Six religious communities are notified as minorities by the Centre.
2. In July 2026, the Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the Centre has notified six minorities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains), and the Ravidassias renewed the separate religion code demand in July 2026.

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Term)
a. Religious pluralism
b. Fundamentalism
c. Revivalism
d. Bhakti movement
List-II (Feature)
i. Rejected ritualism and caste
ii. Forms: communalism, separatism, fanaticism
iii. Arya Samaj's 'Back to the Vedas'
iv. Hindered by exclusivism
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Religious pluralism – hindered by exclusivism (a-iv); fundamentalism – communalism, separatism, fanaticism (b-ii); revivalism – restoring a golden past, 'Back to the Vedas' (c-iii); Bhakti (6th–18th c.) – rejected ritualism and caste (d-i).

s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Thinker)
a. Louis Dumont
b. Max Weber
c. B. Malinowski
d. J.G. Frazer
List-II (Idea)
i. The Religion of India – karma, dharma, caste and economic life
ii. Homo Hierarchicus
iii. The Golden Bough – magic, religion, science
iv. Personal attachments and death as the source of religion
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Louis Dumont – Homo Hierarchicus (a-ii); Weber – The Religion of India (b-i); Malinowski – personal attachments and death (c-iv); Frazer – The Golden Bough, magic → religion → science (d-iii). Homo Hierarchicus is Dumont's, not Malinowski's.

Consider the following statements about the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978:
1. It omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and inserted Article 300A in Part XII.
2. It was passed under the Janata Party government of Morarji Desai.
3. The omission of Article 31 took effect from 20 June 1979.
4. After it, the Constitution contains seven Fundamental Rights.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 3). Statement 4 is wrong: the Fundamental Rights were originally seven and are now six – property is the only FR ever deleted. The 44th (Janata government, Morarji Desai) moved property to Art. 300A, Part XII; Art. 31's omission ran from 20 June 1979.

s:
Assertion (A): The right to property was deleted from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment.
Reason (R): Property rights were the most litigated Fundamental Right and kept blocking land reform and acquisition for public use.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: because property rights kept blocking land reform and acquisition for public use, the 44th Amendment (1978) removed them from Part III.

Consider the following statements about the right to property under Article 300A:
1. It is enforced through Article 226 or an ordinary suit, not Article 32.
2. It is available to any person, including non-citizens and companies.
3. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the right to property was held to be part of the basic structure.
4. In GGR Housing v. State (2026), the AP High Court insisted on strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Kesavananda Bharati held the right to property is not part of the basic structure. Art. 300A is a legal right of any person, enforced via Art. 226 or a suit; GGR Housing (May 2026) stressed strict due process.

2. The right to establish and administer educational institutions belongs only to religious minorities.

x: Statement 2 is wrong: Art. 30(1) covers all minorities, religious or linguistic. It is the 'Charter of Education Rights'; it is not absolute – the right to administer is not a right to maladminister.

4. The right to work under Article 41 is a Directive Principle.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is wrong: Kuldip Nayar (2009) held voting to be only a statutory/legal right. Art. 326 (18+), Sec. 62 RPA 1951 and Art. 41 (DPSP) are correct.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 3 is wrong: the six notified minorities are religious – Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains. The NCM is statutory (1992), and the State is the unit for linguistic minorities (T.M.A. Pai, 2002).

2. Social Impact Assessment is compulsory under it.
3. Compensation can go up to two times the market value in rural areas and four times in urban areas.
4. Acquired land left unused is returned after five years.
How many of the above statements are correct?
x: Only three (1, 2 and 4). Statement 3 is reversed: compensation is up to 4x market value in rural areas and 2x in urban areas. LARR replaced the British 1894 Act, made SIA compulsory and returns unused land after 5 years.
